input.doc_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.doc_summary: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.
input.target_audience: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.parent_summary: Analyze why graph-guided scheduling affects coherence and citation placement, limitations (dataset scale, domain transfer, reliance on retrieval quality), and implications for auditability and reproducibility. Propose mitigations and future extensions.

output.title: Graph-guided scheduling: effects on coherence and citation placement
output.summary: Analyze how leaf-first, dependency-aware ordering influences local and global coherence, rhetorical flow between sections, and the timing/location of evidence citations; identify scenarios where graph structure most improves citation clustering or clarity and where it can introduce disconnects between sections.

output.title: Limitations, failure modes, and practical mitigations
output.summary: Discuss limitations such as small dataset scale, domain-transfer risks, and dependence on retrieval quality; enumerate practical mitigations (data augmentation, retrieval re-ranking, human-in-the-loop checks) and short-term validation strategies to detect and reduce unsupported assertions.

output.title: Implications for auditability, reproducibility, and future work
output.summary: Describe how JSON-constrained outputs and explicit evidence injection improve auditability and reproducibility; propose extensions (richer graph encodings, multi-stage retrieval, evaluation on larger/other domains) and outline next steps for tooling and evaluation to facilitate community adoption.
